name: Object Lifetime, RAII, and the Rules of Three, Five, and Zero
subject: Object-Oriented Programming Systems

mcqs.question: What bug occurs if a class managing dynamically allocated heap memory uses the default compiler-generated copy constructor?
options: Double deletion / double free when both objects destruct
mcqs.explanation: The default copy constructor performs a shallow (bitwise) copy of the pointer. When both instances go out of scope, both destructors attempt to delete the same heap memory address, causing a double free crash.

mcqs.question: What is the "Rule of Zero" in modern C++?
options: All member variables must be initialized to 0 in constructor body
A class should have zero member functions
Classes should rely on RAII types and declare zero custom copy/move/destructor member functions
Virtual functions must have zero runtime overhead
mcqs.explanation: The Rule of Zero states that classes should manage no resources directly, delegating resource ownership to types like std::string or std::vector, so that none of the 5 special member functions need to be declared.

mcqs.question: Why must move constructors be marked with `noexcept`?
options: To allow compilers to eliminate all pointers from the class
To allow std::vector reallocations to safely move elements instead of falling back to copying
To prevent derived classes from overriding the constructor
mcqs.explanation: If a move constructor is not noexcept, std::vector cannot guarantee strong exception safety during reallocations and will revert to copy constructors, degrading performance.
